overview: Suncorp Group is a Brisbane-headquartered, ASX-listed Trans-Tasman general insurer operating through well-recognised brands including AAMI, GIO, Suncorp Insurance, Apia, Shannons and Vero (Australia and New Zealand). Following the completion of the sale of Suncorp Bank to ANZ (31 July 2024) and the earlier divestment of its NZ life insurance business, Suncorp is now a pure-play general insurer with three portfolios: Consumer Insurance, Commercial & Personal Injury Insurance, and Suncorp New Zealand. The balance sheet shrank from ~$112bn total assets pre-sale to ~$30bn as a standalone insurer, with surplus capital progressively returned to shareholders via a $3.00/share capital return plus special dividends (2025) and ongoing buybacks (FY26/FY27).

business_model.summary: Suncorp earns gross written premium (GWP) across home, motor, commercial, workers' compensation, CTP (compulsory third-party/personal injury) and New Zealand consumer/commercial lines, underwrites the risk while ceding a portion via a large reinsurance/catastrophe program, and earns net investment income on shareholder and insurance (float) funds. Revenue is largely recurring (annual policy renewals) with premium rate increases (AWP growth) and unit growth as the main organic growth levers, offset by claims costs (including natural hazard/catastrophe events) and reinsurance costs.
business_model.customer_type: B2C (Consumer home/motor via direct and broker channels) and B2B/institutional (Commercial, Workers' Compensation, CTP via brokers and partners; NZ intermediated via Vero brokers)
business_model.geographic_mix: Australia (Consumer + Commercial & Personal Injury) approximately 84% of FY26 GWP ($13.0bn of $15.4bn), New Zealand (Vero/AA Insurance) approximately 16% (NZ$2.76bn)

competitive_position.market_position: Second-largest general insurer in Australia by GWP (~27% share, behind IAG's ~29% post-RACQ acquisition); IAG, Suncorp, QBE and Allianz collectively control ~74% of the Australian general insurance market. Suncorp is a top-tier player in NZ through Vero (intermediated) and AA Insurance (JV with NZ Automobile Association, direct).

moat_factors.description: AAMI, GIO, Suncorp Insurance, Apia, Shannons, Bingle span multiple customer segments and price points, capturing demand across the market without cannibalizing a single brand's positioning

moat_factors.factor: Scale and data advantage in pricing/underwriting
moat_factors.description: Scale enables sophisticated risk-based pricing and portfolio quality management (e.g., shifting Home book toward lower-risk properties), which has driven margin improvement
Direct-to-consumer digital channels (74.2% digital sales) complemented by broker/partner networks for Commercial and NZ intermediated business
Large reinsurance program plus new multi-year aggregate cover caps downside natural hazard volatility to ~$50m in 90% of scenarios for FY27, a structural advantage smaller insurers cannot replicate
Exclusive relationship with the New Zealand Automobile Association gives Vero/AA Insurance a trusted direct-to-consumer channel in NZ

weaknesses: Trails IAG in overall Australian market share and lacks IAG's scale post-RACQ acquisition
Elevated and rising natural hazard/reinsurance cost base structurally pressures margins in high-catastrophe years
Legacy technology stack requiring a multi-year, ~$560m 'Digital Insurer' platform modernisation program (execution risk)
NZ segment facing GWP contraction (-4.8% FY26) from a soft commercial cycle and weaker economic backdrop
Now a narrower, single-industry (general insurance) earnings base post bank divestment, removing prior diversification

growth_drivers: Continued premium rate increases (AWP growth) and unit growth in Home and Motor, targeting improved portfolio quality (more low-risk homes)
FY27 GWP growth guidance of 3-5% reflecting ongoing pricing to cover inflation in Consumer and Personal Injury, partially offset by soft commercial market

'Digital Insurer' platform modernisation (~$560m spend through FY27, built on Duck Creek core policy administration) and embedded GenAI (20+ initiatives) to reduce cost-to-serve and improve claims speed/accuracy
Direct AA Insurance (NZ) growth in Home and Motor (+3.2% FY26) as a bright spot within a softer NZ market
Capital management: ongoing buybacks ($400m completed FY26, further $250m planned FY27) and special dividends returning surplus capital above CET1 target range to shareholders
CTP/Workers' Compensation pricing tailwinds in NSW and Queensland, and new-business/retention strength in Workers' Compensation
Multi-year aggregate reinsurance cover (from 30 June 2026, up to $800m/yr, $2.4bn over 5 years) reducing earnings volatility and supporting more consistent underlying margins

business.description: FY26 natural hazard costs of $2,024m were $254m above the $1,770m allowance; 32 weather events (18 declared natural hazard events) hit Australia and NZ during the year, including SEQ hailstorms (37,000+ claims) and NZ landslides
Net incurred claims up 10.7% in FY26 on higher natural hazard costs and ongoing claims inflation from construction and labour cost pressure
IAG (larger post-RACQ) and QBE compete aggressively on price and channel; softening commercial insurance cycle in both AU and NZ pressures Commercial and NZ intermediated GWP
Rising premiums amid cost-of-living pressures create political/reputational risk and could cap future rate increases even as claims costs rise

financial.description: Net investment income fell to $553m in FY26 from $766m in FY25 due to mark-to-market losses from rising risk-free rates, despite a higher underlying yield (5.1%)
Reliance on global reinsurance markets for catastrophe protection; hardening reinsurance pricing or reduced capacity would raise costs or reduce coverage
Buybacks and special dividends depend on CET1 remaining above target range; a large catastrophe year or adverse capital shock could curtail planned FY27 returns

regulatory.description: APRA's FY2026-27 Corporate Plan elevates AI-enabled cyber threats, climate-linked affordability pressure and prudential capital requirements as top priorities for insurers

Suncorp participates in APRA's Insurance Climate Vulnerability Assessment (covering ~80% of the AU market); rising uninsured/underinsured household rates increase risk of future government intervention (e.g., cyclone reinsurance pool, price caps)

regulatory.risk: General Insurance Code of Practice changes
regulatory.description: Evolving industry code and claims-handling conduct requirements add compliance costs, particularly around supply chain and repairer standards

macro.description: Structural increase in frequency/severity of cyclones, floods, bushfires and hailstorms across Australia and NZ is the dominant secular risk to underwriting profitability
Investment portfolio yield benefits from higher bond yields (5.1% underlying yield in FY26), but rising risk-free rates simultaneously generate mark-to-market losses on fixed income holdings
Elevated building material and labour costs increase home and motor claims severity, a key driver of the FY26 claims inflation
Weaker NZ economic backdrop and soft commercial insurance cycle directly reduced Suncorp NZ GWP (-4.8%) and margins in H2 FY26

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Australian general insurance industry entering FY27 with underwriting margins broadly restored after a multi-year repricing cycle; all three majors (IAG, SUN, QBE) now returning excess capital via buybacks/dividends. Climate-driven catastrophe losses and reinsurance costs remain the dominant secular headwind, partially offset by continued premium rate increases and improved risk selection.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - general insurance demand is relatively non-discretionary (compulsory motor/CTP, mortgage-linked home insurance) providing revenue stability, but underwriting profitability is highly cyclical around natural catastrophe years and the broader premium pricing cycle (hard vs soft market)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - higher rates lift running yield on the investment portfolio (5.1% underlying AU yield in FY26) but generate near-term mark-to-market losses on bonds as rates rise; also affects claims liability discounting

recent_developments.event: FY26 results: statutory NPAT of $1,027m (down from FY25's bank/NZ-life-sale-boosted result), cash earnings $1,042m, underlying earnings up 4.5% to $1,636m; GWP $15,407m (+2.7%); underlying insurance trading ratio 11.8% (top of 10-12% target range)

Board declared 52cps fully franked final dividend (69cps total FY26 ordinary dividends, 70.5% payout ratio of cash earnings) plus a 10cps fully franked special dividend; announced a further $250m on-market buyback for FY27, following the $400m buyback completed in FY26
Announced FY27 reinsurance program placement and FY27 natural hazard allowance increase to $1,800m (excl. claims handling/profit commission), up from $1,770m in FY26

Placed a new five-year, multi-year aggregate reinsurance cover (up to $800m/year, $2.4bn cumulative limit over 5 years) effective from 30 June 2026, capping FY27 natural hazard downside to ~$50m in 90% of scenarios
CEO Steve Johnston took temporary medical leave; CFO Jeremy Robson appointed acting CEO and EGM Neil Wesley appointed acting CFO during the period

Series of natural hazard events including SEQ hailstorms causing 37,000+ home, motor and commercial claims; contributed to natural hazard costs of $2,024m for FY26, exceeding the $1,770m allowance by $254m
New Board Chairman Duncan West took over following the FY25 AGM
Yen Saw appointed to the Board as a non-executive director (insurance/reinsurance and digital transformation background), seeking election at the FY26 AGM (Sept 2026)
Completed $3.00/share capital return (~$3.8bn) plus special dividend and share consolidation, distributing net proceeds from the Suncorp Bank sale to ANZ (completed 31 July 2024)
Opened AI/satellite-imagery-powered Disaster Management Centre in Brisbane to speed catastrophe damage assessment and claims processing

items.notes: Reflects continued pricing for inflation in Consumer and Personal Injury, partly offset by soft Commercial market conditions in AU and NZ

items.notes: Includes the impact of the new aggregate reinsurance premium; incorporates expected offsets from profit commissions, main catastrophe program savings, loss-ratio initiatives and selective pricing

FY26 payout ratio was 70.5% of cash earnings, positioned around the middle of the target range

guidance.management_commentary: Chairman Duncan West and CEO Steve Johnston both emphasized the resilience of the 'simpler, more focused pure-play insurer' two years post-bank-sale, citing top-of-range underlying margins despite a $254m natural hazard overrun, offset by strong prior-year reserve releases. Management highlighted the new multi-year aggregate reinsurance cover as materially de-risking FY27 natural hazard volatility, and reaffirmed disciplined capital management (special dividend + buyback) as CET1 sits above the target operating range. CEO commentary flagged continued investment in the Digital Insurer platform (Duck Creek core system rollout across Australian brands in FY27) and AI/GenAI at scale as central to reducing cost-to-serve and addressing insurance affordability.

bull_case: Now a focused, simpler pure-play Trans-Tasman insurer post-bank sale, with underlying margins sustained at the top of the 10-12% UITR target range despite a heavy natural hazard year
Disciplined, ongoing capital return program (special dividends + buybacks) supported by CET1 comfortably above target, returning surplus capital directly to shareholders
New five-year aggregate reinsurance cover structurally reduces natural hazard earnings volatility, capping downside to ~$50m in ~90% of FY27 scenarios and improving earnings predictability
Continued premium rate increases and improved risk selection (more low-risk homes) are driving portfolio quality and margin improvement in Consumer Insurance
Multi-brand distribution (AAMI, GIO, Apia, Shannons, Vero) plus digital/AI investment (74%+ digital sales, 20+ GenAI initiatives) support both growth and structural cost-out over time
bear_case: Structurally rising natural hazard and reinsurance costs (FY26 costs of $2,024m, up 49% YoY, exceeding the allowance) reflect a worsening climate risk trend that could persistently pressure margins
Goldman Sachs and other analysts have flagged 'peak margins' and full valuation concerns (consensus rating mostly Hold, average target ~$19-20 vs recent trading levels), limiting re-rating upside
New Zealand segment GWP declined 4.8% in FY26 on a soft commercial cycle and weaker economy, a drag on group growth with no clear near-term catalyst for recovery
Execution risk on the multi-year, ~$560m Digital Insurer/Duck Creek platform modernisation program, which must deliver promised cost-to-serve reductions to sustain margins as pricing tailwinds fade

CEO's temporary medical leave (though resolved) and ongoing board renewal introduce near-term leadership/succession uncertainty; loss of the diversified bank earnings stream leaves Suncorp more exposed to a single-industry (general insurance) catastrophe/pricing cycle
